items.title: ASX falls as oil prices amp up pressure on markets; CSL names new chair
paras: The S&P/ASX 200 was down 64.9 points or 0.7 per cent, to 8730.3 in early trade. Wall Street lost ground on Friday as oil prices hit their highest mark in four years.

Bloomberg CSL has named its interim chief executive Gordon Naylor as its next chair, replacing Brian McNamee, who will end his decades-long association with the Australian pharmaceutical giant. Naylor will take over as chair on March 31.

He will hand over CEO duties to Deborah Waterhouse in February. McNamee, CSL’s former CEO, helped steer the company’s transformation from a government agency into one of Australia’s largest listed companies, but it has struggled with a string of downgrades over the past year which sent its shares sharply lower. On Wall Street on Friday, the S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent as the index posted its second-straight weekly loss.

items.title: India’s private sector activity hits four-month high as inflation cools: HSBC Flash India PMI
paras: India’s private-sector activity grew at its fastest pace in four months in October, with the composite PMI rising to 56.7 from 55.9.

According to HSBC’s Flash India Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI), released on Friday, firms secured higher volumes of new business and remained optimistic about the year-ahead outlook due to easing of inflationary pressure.

The flash survey, an advance estimate ahead of the final PMI readings, offers an early indication of shifts in economic sentiment and output. The HSBC Flash India PMI Composite Output Index, a seasonally adjusted measure of month-on-month changes in the combined output of India’s manufacturing and services sectors compiled by S&P Global, rose to 56.7 in October from 55.9 in September. The reading pointed to a marked expansion in business activity and the fastest growth since June.

items.title: ASX Runners of the Week: Energy Technologies, RAS Tech & Tambourah
paras: Not because markets are suddenly looking rosy, but because fear has become the dominant trade. The unending Middle East conflict has punters too rattled to hold stocks over the weekend, preferring to sell on Friday and buy back on Monday rather than cop another gut-punch from the world news in between.

In much the same fashion, Wall Street fired up to start the week, with better-than-expected results from SpaceX giving the AI trade another sugar hit. Revenue surged 161 per cent to US$14.6 billion, with a US$4.4 billion profit comfortably beating expectations and helping chip stocks and technology names lead the early charge.

This week’s Bulls N’ Bears ASX Runner of the Week is… Energy Technologies. That was about where the good news ended. The Middle East, oil prices, inflation, interest rates and the looming US midterm elections became too much to ignore, combining to build a wall of worry that even the AI bulls are struggling to climb.

items.title: The RBI and its growing fiscal role
paras: Central banks occupy a peculiar position in modern democracies. Central banks, through their toolkit of monetary policy, manage inflation, preserve confidence in the currency, and safeguard financial stability. Their credibility rests on maintaining a degree of distance from the fiscal compulsions of the governments they serve.

items.title: India's Mideast oil imports return to pre-war levels in September
paras: Refiners snapped up spot cargoes as Middle Eastern producers and traders cranked up shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, easing supply constraints caused by the Iran war. The world's third-biggest oil importer initially raised Russian crude imports to compensate for reduced Middle Eastern supplies at the onset of the war.

India's crude imports from the Middle East jumped in September to about 2.8 million barrels per day, the highest since February, up from 32% in August, the data showed. Gulf oil accounted for about 54% of overall imports.

In contrast, Russian oil imports fell about 14% on month to about 1.8 million bpd in September, with its share of India's oil purchases declining to 33.5% from 46.6%, the data showed. Russian oil purchases by Indian refiners are likely to remain subdued in the coming months as the landed cost of Russian oil is now comparable to that of some Middle Eastern grades, mainly Iraqi oil, said an Indian refining source.

items.title: RBI MPC Minutes: Governor Sanjay Malhotra ties future hikes to growth-inflation outlook — here is what he said
paras: The RBI's MPC meeting minutes showed that 37% of commodities in the basket recorded inflation above 4% in August, compared with just 20% in March. The MPC met from October 5 to 7, when all six members voted to increase the benchmark repo rate by 25 basis points (bps) to 5.5%.

The increase marked the first rate hike in nearly four years, reflecting growing concerns about persistent price pressures. RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said the duration and extent of the rate-hiking cycle would depend on actual economic growth and inflation developments, as well as their outlook.

“The extent and duration of the tightening cycle would depend on how growth and inflation evolve,” particularly underlying price pressures and signs that the supply shock is spreading more broadly, he said. Malhotra highlighted increasing signs that inflation was spreading across the consumer price index (CPI) basket.
items.impact: The RBI's MPC meeting minutes showed that 37% of commodities in the basket recorded inflation above 4% in August, compared with just 20% in March.

items.title: RBI MPC minutes reveal 2 members opposed shift from neutral stance to calibrated tightening in October meeting
paras: RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra also announced a shift in the monetary policy committee's stance from neutral to calibrated tightening. While all six MPC members unanimously voted to raise the repo rate by 25 bps as anticipated by the industry, Nagesh Kumar and Ram Singh opposed the shift in stance, the RBI MPC minutes revealed on Wednesday.

Ram Singh - were of the view that the stance be retained at neutral,” the release read. Meanwhile, Malhotra supported shifting the MPC’s stance towards calibrated tightening, citing rising inflationary pressures.

He said that headline CPI is projected to touch the upper tolerance band in the third quarter and remain significantly above 5% in the following two quarters. He also noted that underlying inflation is expected to move above the target in the coming months.

items.title: Indian markets snap 1-week rally following surge in crude, FII outflows
paras: Foreign institutional investors remain net sellers in Indian equities. Indian markets declined on Friday (October 23, 2026), snapping the one-week rally, with most indices ending in red following a surge in crude prices and foreign fund outflows.

Sensex plunged over 1% during the day before settling at 73,123.83, down 125.56 points from its previous close. Nifty declined to the 22,400 level before unwinding some losses and ended at 22,600, down 87.65 points or 0.4%.

Selling pressure remained broad-based, with the broader market witnessing a sharper decline than the frontline indices,” Pabitro Mukherjee, deputy vice-president- Research, Bajaj Broking said in a note. Brent crude prices hit an over 5-month high of $114.6 per barrel, up 1% from the previous close, after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia.

items.title: Record growth, rising risks: What’s really driving India’s core industries? | The Hindu Editorial
paras: India’s core industrial sectors recorded a series-high growth rate of 7.9% in September, driven by strong performances in coal, electricity, steel and refinery products. While the data points to a welcome industrial uptick, concerns remain about how sustainable the momentum will be.

Much of the growth appears linked to temporary factors such as increased power demand during the heat wave and higher refining activity driven by imported oil. With global crude prices rising, foreign exchange pressures mounting and infrastructure spending continuing to shoulder much of the growth burden, economists are questioning whether the current surge can be sustained in the coming months.

Friendships are built by repeated contact, not by being liked
items.hook: This is the single most useful fact in the whole guide.
paras: Studies of primary-school classrooms found that children seated next to each other were far more likely to become friends than children seated across the room. When teachers changed the seating, new friendships formed with the new neighbours.

So the engine is: same place, same people, same activity, over and over. The day at the yo-yo bar followed by basketball is that engine working - shared activity changed how the other boy treated him. It was not luck.
items.do: Pick one activity he already likes and commit to it weekly for a full term.

items.title: Keep the proximity - change the watching
items.hook: Your instinct is half right, and the other half matters.
paras: You are right that being around the group matters: children nominate as friends the children they see and interact with most. 'Out of sight, out of mind' is real for acquaintances.

But guidance written for schools is blunt: merely remaining beside a group is not friendship. A child who hovers is read as a bystander rather than a player, and it holds him in the one-down position. Watching has a use - but only as the first twenty seconds of joining in, never as the endpoint.
items.do: Keep telling him to stay near the group. Add: 'then take a job in the game'.

items.title: Teach 'watch, then blend'
items.hook: The best way to join a game is not to ask.
paras: Most of us were told to walk up and say 'Can I play?' But that makes everyone stop and look at him, and makes 'no' very easy.

The better sequence, used by people who study play: watch for about twenty seconds to learn the game and where the line is, then slide into the action without stopping it. Take the end of the line. Stand in the outfield. Pick up the ball and pass it back.
items.do: Rehearse it at home in five minutes. Ask him to name the 'easiest job' in each game.

items.title: Host one friend at a time - this is the biggest lever you control
items.hook: The child who invites is rarely short of friends.
paras: Pick a child he has had fun with in the last month, not someone he admires from afar. Invite one person for one to two hours. Put away anything precious, have two activities ready, start with a snack, and let the guest choose sometimes.
Keep it short and end while they are both still enjoying it. Then leave a few weeks before inviting the same child again, so the invitation can come back to him.
items.do: Text one parent this week and set a date for the school holidays.

items.title: Ask the teacher one specific question
items.hook: Teachers see the playground. Ask them to name names.
paras: Ask two things: who does he play well with, and could he be seated near them or paired with them for group work?
Seating is one of the few levers that reliably creates new friendships, and it is invisible to the children - no one has to know it was arranged.
items.do: Email the teacher this week with those two questions.

items.title: Do not push into a group that is rejecting him
items.hook: Here the advice is the opposite of persistence.
paras: Where a group is actively excluding him, the guidance is to back off - when you back off from people, they can move towards you. Put his energy into two or three other children instead of one closed circle.
Friends in more than one place - school, a club, family friends - also make him far less vulnerable when one group turns cold.
items.do: Help him list three children outside the difficult group he could get to know.

items.title: One or two good friends is the goal - not popularity
paras: Kids need one or two good friends. You do not need to worry about him being the most popular child in the class.
His warmth and kindness are already the raw material. Treat this as coaching a skill, not fixing a fault - if he feels like a project, he will resist.
items.do: Say his strengths out loud, often. Confidence is what carries a child into a group.

items.title: Playing and talking with girls is normal and good
items.hook: Children believe gender matters far more than it actually does.
paras: In one large classroom experiment, simply seating boys and girls next to each other doubled how often they became friends.
Girls' play tends to build conversation, turn-taking and inventing games together; boys' play builds bigger, faster group play. Being good at both widens his circle.
items.do: No action needed. Just do not let him think it is odd.

items.title: When to get more help
items.hook: Ordinary friendship difficulty is not a disorder.
paras: Get more support if he becomes reluctant to go to school, is persistently distressed, has changes in sleep or appetite, or says it is happening all the time and he cannot make it stop.
Start with his teacher, then the school counsellor, then your GP for a referral. Kids Helpline is free and open 24/7 on 1800 55 1800, for children and for parents.
items.do: Save Kids Helpline in your phone: 1800 55 1800.
